title: Governance, DAOs, and Airdrop Dynamics
objectives: See how on-chain governance actually executes a treasury move
Understand the flash-loan governance hijack well enough to recognise the pattern
Know why timelocks and vote-escrow exist
Read an airdrop as a liquidity event rather than a gift

steps.title: Decentralization vs. Coordination
steps.body:
DeFi protocols want to avoid a single point of failure, so instead of a board of directors they deploy on-chain governance — on Solana, typically through SPL Governance or Realms. Token holders propose changes, vote on them, and execute parameter updates and treasury payments through the program.

It sounds clean. In practice, naive token-weighted voting creates economic attack surfaces that can empty an entire treasury if the rules are loose enough. This lesson is about those surfaces and the defences that close them.

steps.title: The Flash Loan Governance Hijack
steps.body:
Take a DAO with a $20M treasury and 10,000,000 governance tokens. Ordinary participation is low — often only 5% to 8% of supply votes on a routine proposal.

Now suppose the system executes a passed vote immediately:

1. An attacker notices that a quiet weekend proposal drew only 500,000 votes.
2. In a single transaction, they borrow 1,000,000 governance tokens from a lending market or AMM.
3. They vote yes on a proposal that transfers $10M of treasury to their own wallet.
4. It passes quorum, executes, and the borrowed tokens go back in the same block.

This is a <Term id="flash_loan">flash loan</Term> <Term id="governance">governance</Term> hijack, and it is not theoretical. Beanstalk lost about $182M this way on Ethereum in April 2022, and Build Finance was taken the same month. The <Term id="dao">DAO</Term> never had a chance to react, because the entire attack fit inside one transaction.

steps.title: Institutional Defenses: Timelocks & Multisig Councils
steps.body:
Battle-tested protocols stack several layers so a hijack cannot become a withdrawal.

- **Execution timelocks, 24 to 72 hours.** Once a vote passes, nothing moves until the delay expires. If a malicious proposal passes, users and LPs can read it and withdraw their capital before execution.
- **Security councils and veto multisigs.** Community guardians hold multisig keys able to cancel proposals that break the protocol's rules. Squads on Solana is the common implementation.
- **Vote-escrowed locking.** Only tokens locked for one to four years carry voting power. Flash-borrowed tokens cannot be locked, so they cannot vote. The attack dies at step two.

The pattern across all three: make vote-buying expensive or slow enough that honest participants have time to exit.

steps.title: The Airdrop Flywheel & The Mercenary Dump
steps.body:
<Term id="airdrop">Airdrops</Term> are crypto's primary user-acquisition tool: reward early community members with governance tokens and you get attention, holders, and a story. The secondary market math is less romantic.

- **The mercenary sell-off.** A large share of recipients sell their entire allocation on day one for SOL or stablecoins. They farmed the airdrop; they are not here for the product.
- **Sybil industrialisation.** Professional farmers run scripts across thousands of wallets to multiply claims. Protocols respond with on-chain clustering heuristics that prune sybil rings before the snapshot.
- **Retention design.** Modern protocols fight the dump with staking multiplier boosts, fee sharing, or phased <Term id="vesting">vesting</Term> on the claim itself — anything that makes selling on day one costly.

Read an airdrop as a liquidity event, not a gift. The size of the claim, the cliff on it, and the depth of the receiving pool tell you more than the announcement does.

steps.title: Under the Hood: Multisig Governance on Solana with Squads
steps.body:
On Solana, institutional governance mostly runs through Squads, a multisig program used by protocols and foundations to hold upgrade authorities and treasuries.

The core is a simple threshold: an M-of-N rule, such as 4 of 7 signers, must approve any transaction the vault executes. Around that sit the operational controls teams actually rely on:

- Automated timelocks so a fully signed transaction still waits before it can run.
- Spending limits per account, so a compromised key cannot empty a vault on its own.
- Program upgrade authority held by the vault rather than an individual, so shipping a change also requires the threshold.

The security property worth remembering: a multisig does not make a bad proposal impossible, it makes a unilateral one impossible. Combine it with a timelock and you get both the threshold and the exit window — which is what actually stops the flash-loan hijack from mattering.

questions.prompt: Why is an on-chain execution timelock (e.g. 48-72 hours) essential for DAO governance security?
options: It gives validators time to pause the blockchain
It gives liquidity providers and users a window to review passed proposals and withdraw their funds if a malicious takeover occurred
It speeds up transaction throughput by 400%
It eliminates gas fees for all voters
questions.explainRight: A timelock does not stop a bad vote; it slows it down. Between passage and execution, LPs and users can read the proposal, see the treasury transfer, and leave. That exit window is the defence.
questions.explainWrong: Validators cannot pause the chain, it does not speed anything up, and it has nothing to do with fees. The delay exists so honest capital can withdraw before a malicious proposal can move funds.

questions.prompt: How does vote-escrow locking (veTokenomics) neutralize flash-loan governance attacks?
options: It requires users to submit government IDs to vote
Only tokens locked in a smart contract for months or years receive voting weight, making single-block borrowed tokens completely powerless
It reduces the voting quorum to 0%
questions.explainRight: Flash loans last for a single transaction. Tokens locked for months or years cannot be borrowed for one block, so the borrowed balance carries no voting weight and the attack fails before it can reach the treasury.
questions.explainWrong: No KYC and no banned swaps. Time-locked vote escrow measures commitment in months and years, which single-block borrowed tokens cannot fake.

questions.prompt: What typically happens to token price and liquidity in the first 48 hours after a large unvested public airdrop claim goes live?
options: Heavy retail sell pressure occurs as mercenary farmers monetize rewards, requiring deep DEX liquidity to prevent sharp drawdowns
The token automatically converts into Solana native gas
All liquidity pools are permanently deleted
questions.explainRight: An unvested airdrop is free money to most recipients, and mercenary farmers sell it. The first hours are a stress test for the AMM: if the pool is thin, the claim itself becomes the dump.
questions.explainWrong: Recipients do not hold forever, nothing converts to gas, and pools are not deleted. Unvested airdrops generate substantial immediate sell pressure from short-term farmers.
